questions.q: How does this lesson define technical debt?
options: A synonym for incompetent or careless work
A formal Salesforce licensing fee for using legacy automation tools
The deferred cost of a shortcut taken now in exchange for faster delivery, which accrues cost the longer it's left unaddressed
Any use of declarative tools instead of Apex
questions.explain: The lesson uses the financial-debt metaphor deliberately: a shortcut taken for speed now, which isn't inherently irresponsible but accrues cost ('interest') the longer it's left unaddressed.

questions.q: According to this lesson, what makes taking on technical debt a reasonable decision rather than a reckless one?
options: Whether the shortcut was taken knowingly, with the limitation documented, rather than discovered by accident by whoever hits it next
Debt is always reckless, with no reasonable version
Whether the shortcut involves Apex rather than Flow
Whether the shortcut was approved by a Technical Architect specifically
questions.explain: The lesson distinguishes deliberate debt (knowingly taken, documented) from reckless debt (undocumented, discovered by accident) -- the distinction is about visibility and intent, not the shortcut itself.

questions.q: Why does this lesson name old Process Builder and Workflow Rules processes left running after Salesforce's retirement of those tools as a specific source of technical debt?
options: Because they are completely unrelated to technical debt as a concept
Because Process Builder and Workflow Rules were never actually retired by Salesforce
Because they only affect Experience Cloud sites
Because they represent legacy automation left in place 'because it still works,' carrying real, specific debt with a known deadline pressure behind their eventual retirement
questions.explain: Process Builder and Workflow Rules were retired and needed migration to Flow; leaving old versions running alongside newer automation is a concrete, named example of legacy automation debt.

questions.q: What does this lesson identify as the single most important discipline for managing technical debt?
options: Eliminating all technical debt before any feature can ship
Making debt visible -- documenting what the shortcut is, why it was taken, and what would trigger revisiting it -- rather than letting it live only in the memory of whoever created it
Hiring more developers to prevent debt from ever being created
Refusing to ever take on debt under any business constraint
questions.explain: The lesson emphasizes visibility: a short, living record of what the shortcut is and why it was taken turns invisible risk into a known, manageable, prioritizable item.

questions.q: Per this lesson, what question should an architect ask during a design review regarding technical debt?
options: Whether the design uses Flow instead of Apex
Whether the design passed user acceptance testing
What debt is this design knowingly taking on, and is it written down anywhere -- treating a clean-looking design as evidence that no trade-offs were made is a mistake
Whether the design used a managed package
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly recommends this question as a standard part of design review (Lesson 20), warning against assuming a clean-looking design made no trade-offs at all.
